thread.title: It's been a couple of days now since Apple ( AAPL ) reported

author: Bill Maurer
title: It's been a couple of days now since Apple ( AAPL ) reported
text:
It's been a couple of days now since Apple ( AAPL ) reported its fiscal first quarter earnings. When I had my initial reaction piece posted, shares were down in the after-hours, but soon rallied as the evening went on. Unfortunately, things turned ugly on Friday with a market rout, with concerns over Apple's growth causing a lot of selling. Fortunately, this gives investors a chance to reset their expectations, which could be a good setup for the future.
I think part of the problem with the earnings report was that the headline of declining iPhone sales over the prior year period. While that fact was true on a numerical basis, last year's quarter had an extra week, and management had to remind everyone on the conference call numerous times that the extra week obviously plays a big role in terms of growth rates. All three main product lines showed unit sales declines, but that wouldn't have been the case if we adjusted last year's period. The same goes for growth rates in services and other products.
It now appears that there will not be this large iPhone supercycle this year that many were hoping for. However, one analyst suggests that it's actually better that this does not happen, mainly because it would create one big year that drives expectations too high and can't be repeated in following years. Under this theory, Apple has an elongated, multi-year upgrade cycle. So instead of having like 30% growth and then two flat years, you have three years of 10% growth. Would that be such a bad thing?
If Apple truly wants to spark massive unit growth in the coming years, I've long argued it will need to come down the price ladder a bit. New versions of the iPhone SE, the iPad mini, etc. are the perfect outlets to this strategy, and they can be done at price points that don't kill margins. While it was nice to see huge increases in device average selling prices in the latest quarter, those gains are not sustainable in the long term.
